creative.body:
If you're going 3, 4, even 5 days between bowel movements since you started Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro or Zepbound, it's not because you need more fiber, more water, or more salads.

My name is Dr. Rebecca Marsh.

I'm a gastroenterologist, and I've spent the last 18 years specializing in gut motility disorders. The medical term for the speed at which food moves through your digestive system.

It's a quiet corner of medicine. Most of my training was for patients with diabetic gastroparesis, post-surgical motility complications, and the rare hereditary motility syndromes that affect maybe 1 in 10,000 people. I expected to spend my career in that quiet corner.

Then GLP-1 medication went mainstream.

I'm writing this for the people on a GLP-1 medication who have quietly accepted the bloating, the 4-day stretches, the pants that stop fitting by dinner, and the shot-day dread as the cost of finally losing the weight.

If you'll hear me out, I can explain something the doctor who wrote your prescription never had the time to. Something every online article, every Reddit thread, and every well-meaning "have you tried more fiber" comment has missed completely.

You know what I'm about to describe.

You know the 4-day stretches. You know the pressure that sets in under your ribs by lunch. You know the shot-day dread, the way you start clearing your calendar 36 hours before the injection. You know the bathroom math. What you can eat, when, and how long you have before the bloating turns into something worse. You know what it feels like to look at a plate of food your husband made for dinner and feel something close to fear.

I want to explain why none of the advice you've been given has helped.

Over the last 3 years in my practice, I've watched the same story play out again and again.

A patient starts the shot.

The weight starts coming off.

Within a few weeks, their digestion falls apart.

These are patients who have done everything they've been told to do.

Who have doubled their fiber.

Who are drinking so much water they can't sleep through the night.

Who have packed every meal with leafy greens.

Who have tried Miralax, Metamucil, Dulcolax, psyllium husk, magnesium citrate, 3 different probiotics, and a drawerful of digestive enzymes.

And who still wake up bloated, distended, and unable to pass anything for 4, 5, sometimes 6 days at a stretch.

I've had patients in my exam room in tears, telling me they've started skipping meals not because they aren't hungry but because the pressure of food sitting on top of food on top of food has become unbearable.

I've had patients tell me they've stopped going out to eat with their families because they don't trust their bodies to make it through a meal without the bloating turning into something worse.

I've had patients who came to me already on the verge of quitting the medication. People who had lost 40, 50, 60 pounds. Whose blood sugar had finally normalized. Whose joints had stopped hurting for the first time in a decade. And who were ready to throw the pen in the trash because the constipation and the bloating had become more miserable than the weight itself ever was.

At some point I started to understand these patients didn't need more fiber.

They didn't need another laxative.

They needed someone to explain what was actually happening to their stomach the moment that medication entered their system.

GLP-1 medications work by slowing your stomach down.

That isn't a side effect. That's the medication doing exactly what it was designed to do, holding food in your stomach longer so you feel full on less.

The weight loss depends on that slowdown.

But here's what nobody explained when you were handed the prescription.

Your stomach is now emptying at a fraction of the speed it used to.

Food that would normally leave your stomach in 2 hours is now sitting there for 5, 6, sometimes 8.

Every meal lands on top of the meal before it.

Nothing is flowing through. Everything is stacking up.

When food sits in a stomach contracting at half speed, 2 things happen.

First, the food begins to ferment. Bacteria that normally live in your gut, specifically bacteria that thrive in the small intestine when food has been sitting too long, get a longer feeding window than they were ever designed to have. They produce sulfur compounds, methane, and hydrogen as byproducts.

That is what your bloating actually is. Not water retention. Not a food intolerance. The gas your own gut bacteria are producing because the food is sitting in your stomach for 3 to 4 times longer than it is supposed to.

Second, the food that finally does move out of your stomach reaches your colon hours late and in a state your colon was not built to receive. Your colon expects partially-broken-down food at a steady, predictable rate. What it is now getting is dumped in irregular waves with too much fermentation already in it.

Your colon, in response, slows its own contractions. It is trying to give your body time to figure out what just arrived. The result is constipation that does not respond to colon-targeted laxatives, because the colon is not the problem. The colon is downstream of the problem.

This is what every piece of dietary advice you've been given has missed.

The standard advice was written for a normal stomach. The standard advice tells you to feed a colon that is sluggish from too little fiber. Your colon is not sluggish from too little fiber. Your colon is sluggish because your stomach is sending it signals 6 hours late.

Fiber. Water. Salads. Vegetables. Psyllium husk. Metamucil.

Every single one of them is food. And food requires a moving stomach to do anything for you.

Fiber added to a stomach that has stopped releasing its contents just joins the pile that is already sitting there. Which is why the more fiber you added, the worse the bloating got. Which is why the extra water only made you feel fuller, not more regular. Which is why the salads produced gas and pressure instead of relief.

You weren't failing to follow the advice correctly.

The advice itself was aimed at a problem you don't have.

You don't have a fiber deficiency.

Your stomach has been slowed to a crawl by the medication, and every recommendation you've been handed was designed for a stomach that empties in 2 hours. Yours, as it was before the shot.

Your stomach does not need more food. It needs to start moving what is already sitting there.

There is a compound in celery juice called apigenin.

If you have not heard of it, you are not alone. It is one of the more under-studied flavonoids in modern nutritional science, despite being one of the more abundant compounds in a category of vegetables we have all been eating for centuries.

The research on apigenin shows it supports gastric motility at the exact point where GLP-1s have slowed it down. It does not override the medication. It does not force contractions or create urgency the way a laxative does. It helps the stomach begin doing what it has stopped doing on its own.

The mechanism is documented. Apigenin acts on the receptors that govern smooth muscle contraction in the stomach wall. It does not bypass the GLP-1 medication. It works at a different layer of the same system, gently restoring some of the motility tone the medication has suppressed, without compromising the slowdown that produces the weight loss.

That distinction matters. It is the reason this approach can work for someone on a GLP-1 without undermining the medication itself.

The food that has been stacking up finally moves.

The bloating releases.

The pressure that has been building for days starts to come down.

There is a second piece I want to mention, because it addresses the part of the GLP-1 experience nobody likes to talk about.

The sulfur burps.

If you have had them, you know exactly what I mean. The gassy reflux that tastes like rotten eggs. The kind of burp you cannot predict, cannot suppress, and that makes you afraid to be in a meeting or on a date or in a car with your mother-in-law.

Those burps are a direct product of the fermentation I described earlier. They are the sulfur compounds the bacteria in your stalled stomach are producing. They smell exactly like what they are.

Chlorophyllin is a stabilized form of chlorophyll, the pigment that makes green plants green. It binds to sulfur compounds at the molecular level. It does not mask the smell. It neutralizes the source. The bacteria can keep producing whatever they are producing, but the chlorophyllin chemically deactivates the byproducts before they reach the back of your throat.

The third piece is a small targeted dose of soluble prebiotic fiber.

This is not the bulk-forming fiber your doctor has been telling you to add. The bulk-forming fiber feeds a colon directly, and as I have already explained, your colon does not have a fiber problem. It has a timing problem.

Soluble prebiotic fiber, in a small dose, working downstream inside a digestive tract that is actually moving again, does what fiber was always supposed to do in the first place. It feeds the bacteria in the lower gut that produce butyrate. Butyrate keeps the colon contracting once the stomach starts emptying again. Downstream support, not more bulk packed onto a closed on-ramp.

Apigenin, chlorophyllin, and a targeted dose of soluble prebiotic fiber, working together, address the 3 things actually happening in a slowed stomach.

The motility itself.

The fermentation byproducts.

And the downstream support for the colon once the system is moving again.

I had a patient last October I will call Margaret. 58 years old. On Mounjaro for 7 months. Down 38 pounds. She had not had an unassisted bowel movement in 4 months when she walked into my office.

She had tried Miralax, Metamucil, magnesium citrate, 2 different probiotics, and a stimulant laxative her primary care had reluctantly prescribed. Her bloating was so severe by evening that she had stopped eating dinner with her husband. She told me she was 2 weeks from quitting the medication.

I explained to her what I have just explained to you.

She started the approach the next week.

By day 9 she had her first unassisted bowel movement in 17 weeks.

By week 4 she was eating dinner with her husband again.

She came back to my office in February and told me she had lost another 11 pounds since I had seen her last. The bloating was gone. The shot-day dread was gone. She was not planning her week around her gut anymore.

I have a folder of follow-up notes that say versions of the same thing.

The first week, most patients notice the burps stop. The chlorophyllin works fast. The fermentation gases that were reaching the throat get neutralized within a few days. That is usually the first sign something is shifting.

The second week, the bloating starts to ease. Not gone. Eased. The pressure under the ribs gets lighter. Patients tell me they can sit through a full dinner without changing into elastic pants afterward.

By the end of the second week, most patients have their first unassisted bowel movement.

I want to spend a sentence on what unassisted means. It means waking up and going, the way you used to before any of this started. No magnesium the night before. No Miralax cleanout. No emergency Dulcolax. No suppository. Just a body doing what bodies are supposed to do.

For a lot of my patients, that morning is the first time in 3 or 4 months their body has done that on its own. Several of them have texted me from the bathroom. One emailed me a single word, which I will not include here, but which made me laugh out loud at my desk.

By week 4, the pattern feels reliable. Daily or every-other-day movements. Bloating that does not return by dinner. Shot day comes and goes without the dread.

By month 2, most patients are not thinking about their gut anymore. They are losing weight. They are stepping on the scale. They are putting on clothes that fit. The medication is doing what it was supposed to do, and the constipation is no longer the price.

The product I am referring to is called Motilli. I am not affiliated with the company. I do not have a financial relationship with them. I started recommending it to patients after I saw the formulation, read the research behind each ingredient, and watched the first handful of patients I sent to it come back with results I had not seen from any other approach.

Motilli is built around apigenin from celery juice extract, chlorophyllin, and a targeted dose of soluble prebiotic fiber. The 3 ingredients I just walked you through.

It contains no laxative compounds, no stimulants, and no ingredients that force urgency, cramping, or dependency. There is no rebound the way there is with stimulant laxatives. It does not bind to the GLP-1 receptor, so it does not slow weight loss, it does not change appetite suppression, and it does not undermine the medication. It works at a separate layer of the same system.

Two gummies in the morning. That is the whole protocol.

Motilli offers a 90-day no-questions-asked guarantee. If the bloating, constipation, and shot-day misery have not meaningfully improved in that time, you are fully covered.

I do not think you will need that guarantee. But it is there because anyone who has been told for months to "just eat more fiber" while suffering every single day since their first injection deserves to find out without risking anything further.

One thing I will mention. Motilli is a small company. They batch-produce because apigenin starts to degrade once it is exposed to light and time. Which is why most celery extract products on the shelf do not deliver the effect their labels suggest. They sat in a warehouse too long. Motilli does not keep months of inventory. The trade-off is that batches sell out for stretches at a time, particularly when more women on GLP-1s find them. If they are in stock when you click through, that is the day to order.

If you have read this far, you already know whether what I have described is what is happening to you. You know the 4-day stretches. You know the pressure under your ribs. You know the shot-day dread. You know the elastic pants by dinner.

You also know that nothing you have tried so far has actually addressed the real problem, because nothing you have tried so far was built for the real problem.

The link is below.

Sincerely,

Dr. Rebecca Marsh

Gastroenterology and GI Motility Disorders

P.S. Patients call my office and ask whether they should stay on the medication if it is doing this to their digestion. The medication is not doing this to your digestion. The medication slowed your stomach by design, and nobody told you what to do for the stomach you now have. That is not the same thing as the medication being wrong for you. If it is finally letting you lose weight, quitting it is not the answer. Supporting the stomach the medication has put you in is. The link below is what that looks like.
